title: KV cache eviction sketches and quick experiment plan
content:
Context: quick scratchpad for ideas about KV cache eviction policies and a small experiment plan to validate cost/latency tradeoffs. For hosted and dedicated modes we need something that: (a) respects latency SLOs, (b) reduces redundant compute for repeated prefixes, and (c) is predictable across model variants (quantized vs fp16).

Motivation / the problem:
- KV entries (prefixes) consume GPU memory and slow warmups if we try to keep too many.
- TTL-only eviction leads to occasional cold starts for medium-frequency users (e.g., support chatbots with diurnal patterns).
- LRU can thrash when a small number of long-context sessions dominate and block many short sessions.

High-level goals:
1) Keep warmups for high-value prefixes (by frequency * expected continuation length).
2) Protect short, low-cost requests from being evicted by heavy long sessions (avoid latency regressions).
3) Provide deterministic fallbacks so app teams can reason about tail latency.

Brainstormed policies (ranked quick):
- Weighted LRU (wLRU): score = freq * continuation_length_estimate * model_priority. Evict lowest score.
  - Pro: aligns with business value. Con: needs frequency tracking, slightly more state.
- Segmented cache (hot / warm / cold): small fast segment pinned for short session prefixes; large long-lived segment gated by score.
  - Pro: isolates short-run latency. Con: tuning thresholds hard across workloads.
- Time-decayed popularity (exponential decay on counts): helps adapt to diurnal shifts.
- Cost-aware eviction: estimate per-prefix token-cost saved if kept; evict smallest delta.
- Explicit app pinning via API: allow customers to mark specific prompt families as "pin" in Dedicated/Private (opt-in).

Concrete micro-experiments to run (priority order):
1) Simulated workload replay using prod-sample trace (1 week) against a model of memory occupancy. Compare LRU vs wLRU vs segmented cache. Metrics: p95 latency, p99 latency, cold-start frequency, average tokens-per-eviction. (Owner: me; infra ticket: RINF-2418)
2) Small A/B on Dedicated fleet: 2 nodes with segmented cache, 2 with baseline LRU, route small traffic (10%). Monitor tail latency and cost per token. 48–72h. (Need SRE guardrails and canary limits.)
3) Synthetic microbench: create sessions that alternate between many short requests (<=64 tokens) and a few long sessions (>=2048 tokens) and measure eviction churn.

Notes on implementation details / heuristics:
- Frequency tracker: use approximate counting (Count-Min sketch) to avoid per-prefix heavy state. Periodically reconcile with exact counts from trace replays.
- continuation_length_estimate: collect rolling average of generated tokens by prefix-hash over recent N uses; use clipped mean to avoid outliers.
- model_priority: map model_family -> multiplier (e.g., high-accuracy models get 0.8 cost weight, smaller quantized ones 1.1) to prefer keeping cheap-to-serve variants around for cost optimization.
- Eviction batch size: evict in small batches during low-load windows to avoid cascading cold starts.
- Observability: emit token-saved estimate per-eviction event and a reason tag (age/score/space-pressure) so console can show impact and we can alert on regressions.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How correlated are prefix hashes across customers? If many tenants share prefixes, eviction policy should be global; otherwise tenant-local policies are better for privacy / predictability. Need to check prod trace for prefix overlap. (Action: query trace cluster, assign to Arun.)
- How to handle multi-model fallbacks: if we evict a prefix for a large model but keep a quantized variant, should routing prefer the quantized warm prefix automatically? That introduces semantic differences. Might be ok if we clearly document.
- Cost model accuracy: our token-cost saved estimator needs to account for batching benefits (keeping many prefixes can increase opportunity for batching). Simplified estimator will likely undercount.

Operational guardrails I want in any rollout:
- Auto-roll-back threshold: if p99-latency increases by >15% or error-rate grows >0.5% over baseline, revert.
- Gradual ramp: 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% over at least 72h, with manual sign-off at 25%.
- Telemetry dashboard: eviction rate, avg re-warm time, cost-saved estimate, per-tenant cold-starts.

Quick TODOs / tickets:
- RINF-2418: repro baseline / simulation harness (me).
- RINF-2463: add eviction telemetry tags to runtime (SRE).
- Sync with Product: decide whether "pin via API" is a go or a later Enterprise feature (Lena owns product convo).

Rough sketch (ascii):
[hot segment] size=16MB: store very recent short prefixes -> serve sub-64 token SLO
[warm segment] size=128MB: scored by wLRU -> holds medium prefixes with high score
[cold segment] rest -> TTL-based, cheap entries + offload candidate list

Small notes to self:
- When measuring p99, separate by request token-length buckets (<=64, 65-512, >512) since policy affects them differently.
- Consider API flag: `eviction_hint: keep=true|best-effort` to give apps control without full pin.
- Talk to console team about surfacing "eviction impact" in per-route dashboards.

References / links collected while reading:
- caching and eviction literature notes (local pdfs): confluence:eviction-lit-review
- Slack: #infra-kv-cache has earlier convo from May 2026 re: LRU thrash
- internal eval: rinf-evals/kv-warmup-2026-06 (use for initial scoring heuristics)

End of quick scratchpad. Will iterate after we run the replay and get numbers.

Notes-to-self (brain dump):
- possible experiment variant: constrained memory scenario where we force eviction pressure and measure percent of requests served from warmed KV vs end-to-end token compute cost.
- Keep this file as a single source of truth for early brainstorming; move cleaned proposal to Confluence once we have 1 experiment result.
